title: Searching for a Place
subtitle: Work, Affection and the Search for Belonging · 1869–1881
intro: A home, a livelihood, a relationship, a purpose. Each gives us a way into Vincent’s early life.
wallText: Follow the places and people that shaped these years. Letters preserve particular moments. Family recollections and later research offer further accounts, with questions that remain open.

chapters.title: A New Home
chapters.subtitle: London, 1873
chapters.kicker: A YOUNG MAN, NOT YET A PAINTER
chapters.imageCaption: Vincent van Gogh, aged nineteen. Photograph by J. M. W. de Louw, The Hague, January 1873. Taken before his move to London.
chapters.imageCredit: Original photographic portrait · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: In May 1873, twenty-year-old Vincent van Gogh arrived in London to work for the art dealer Goupil & Cie. By August, he had moved into lodgings at 87 Hackford Road.
His letter to Theo that September introduces not a tragic artist, but a young man pleased with his new surroundings—and eager to share them.

sections.title: A Room and a Household
paragraphs: At Hackford Road, Vincent boarded with the widowed Sarah Ursula Loyer and her daughter, Eugénie. The household also accommodated a small school for boys. For Mrs Loyer, teaching and letting rooms were ways of earning a living.

On 13 September 1873, Vincent described his new room to Theo. He was glad to have left behind the sloping beams and blue wallpaper with a green border of his previous lodgings. He found the household lively and wished his brother could see it.
The same letter moves easily from domestic news to an outing on the Thames and an exhibition of Belgian paintings. Home, companionship and pictures belonged to the same conversation.

quote.text: Oh! Old man, I so want that you come here to see my new lodgings
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 13 September 1873 · Letter 13

chapters.prompt: Look beyond the famous name. What would you want to tell someone about your first home in a new city?

actions.label: Art Before Painting
actions.description: Optional branch · Work and the pictures he chose to share

chapters.evidence: The portrait was taken in January 1873, before London. The letter documents his new room and the boys’ school. The house photograph shown here was taken on 17 May 2016, not in 1873. The letter excerpt is a typeset quotation from WebExhibits, not a manuscript image; its wording differs from the modern scholarly translation.

chapters.title: A Life He Enjoyed
chapters.subtitle: Art, Nature and Everyday Pleasure — 1874
chapters.kicker: PLEASURE ALSO BELONGS IN HIS BIOGRAPHY
paragraphs: At the beginning of 1874, Vincent told Theo that life in London was going well. He enjoyed his home, the city, and the people around him.
His letters leave room for a Vincent often overshadowed by later tragedy: curious, appreciative, and capable of taking pleasure in ordinary things.

views.label: January: Home and Art
views.title: January — A World Worth Looking At
paragraphs: In his January letter, Vincent moves between affection for his brother and enthusiasm for art. He lists painters he admires, praises Millet’s The Angelus, and encourages Theo to keep walking and loving nature.
For him, looking at the world and looking at pictures were connected. Painters could help people notice what they might otherwise overlook.
He also describes the satisfaction of having a comfortable home, alongside nature, art and poetry. Read this letter before the accounts of disappointment: happiness, too, belongs in his biography.

quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, beginning of January 1874 · Letter 17

views.label: April: Gardens and Walks
views.title: April — A Garden and a Walk
paragraphs: By 30 April, Vincent was writing about flowering gardens and magnificent chestnut trees. He had sown sweet peas, poppies and mignonette, and was waiting to see what would grow.
He enjoyed walking between home and the office, a journey he estimated at about forty-five minutes. Yet pleasure in London coexisted with longing for Holland, especially Helvoirt.
These details need not become symbols of his future paintings. They matter first as the activities and attachments of a young man living away from home.

quote.text: He that sincerely loves nature, finds pleasure everywhere.
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 30 April 1874 · Letter 22

chapters.prompt: What changes when we give his happiness as much attention as his suffering?

chapters.title: An Uncertain Attachment
chapters.subtitle: Affection, Disappointment and an Incomplete Record
paragraphs: Did Vincent fall in love at Hackford Road?

A later family memoir tells of an attachment that was not returned. Research has revisited the woman’s identity and the sequence of events. The familiar story of heartbreak survives—but not as a fully documented scene.

sections.title: A Story Told Afterwards
paragraphs: In Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s retrospective account, Vincent confessed his love to a woman she called Ursula. She was already engaged to a previous lodger. Jo describes his unsuccessful attempts to change her mind, followed by withdrawal and growing religious preoccupation.
This is a family account written afterwards, not Vincent’s own description of a confession. It gives the episode emotional force, but should not be read as a transcript of what happened.

Van Gogh House London takes a more cautious approach: it describes his affection for Eugénie as rumoured and acknowledges that the circumstances of his departure remain unclear. Family correspondence expresses concern, but does not settle every question.
Here, the story is presented as an unresolved part of his life—not a single explanation for everything that followed.

chapters.prompt: A shared address connects people. Does it also prove the story later told about them?

actions.label: Compare the Accounts
actions.description: Letters · Family memory · Later research · What remains uncertain

chapters.evidence: This original relationship card is a reading aid, not a historic document or a picture of a proven couple. Samuel Plowman is the man Eugénie married in 1878; identifying him as the earlier fiancé remains an interpretation. The reported engagement comes from Bailey’s account of Anna’s correspondence, not a manuscript displayed here.

chapters.title: Sources & Versions
chapters.subtitle: How Do We Know This Story?
paragraphs: A letter, a family memoir and a later interpretation do not speak from the same position.
This display separates what Vincent wrote, what others remembered, and what researchers have inferred. Different accounts remain visible without being treated as equally certain.

evidenceCards.title: Letters
evidenceCards.label: CONTEMPORARY CORRESPONDENCE
paragraphs: The letters displayed here describe a new room, a pleasant home, paintings, gardening and daily walks. They give us Vincent’s own account of these parts of his London life.
They do not narrate a romantic confession or rejection. Their silence cannot establish that nothing happened; equally, it does not allow us to supply the missing conversation.

evidenceCards.title: Family Recollections
evidenceCards.label: RETROSPECTIVE FAMILY ACCOUNT
paragraphs: Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s memoir presents disappointed love as a turning point. Her account links the episode with changes in Vincent’s behaviour and an increasingly religious life.
It preserves a family understanding of his experience. Yet it was written retrospectively, and its naming of the woman as Ursula has become part of the historical debate.
Read it as an influential account—not an eyewitness record of the encounter.

evidenceCards.title: Later Research
evidenceCards.label: LATER RESEARCH & INTERPRETATION
paragraphs: In 2019, Van Gogh specialist Martin Bailey revisited the story using census information and correspondence from Vincent’s sister Anna. He argues that Eugénie, rather than her mother, was the likely object of Vincent’s affection.
Bailey reports that Anna’s February 1874 correspondence already mentioned Eugénie’s engagement. This complicates a narrative in which Vincent first discovered it during a confession in August.

Eugénie married Samuel Plowman in 1878. Bailey considers him the likely earlier fiancé, but does not regard that identification as certain. This is a named specialist’s research article, not a peer-reviewed paper.

evidenceCards.title: Open Questions
evidenceCards.label: UNRESOLVED · CURATORIAL PERSPECTIVE
paragraphs: The accounts assembled here do not establish the exact words, date or circumstances of a confession, or fully explain Vincent’s departure.

Some narratives connect disappointed love with his turn towards religion. That connection is an interpretation, not a demonstrated psychological cause. Van Gogh House explicitly leaves the circumstances of his departure unresolved.
Uncertainty is not an invitation to invent a scene. It is a reason to leave space around the people involved.

chapters.prompt: Which details come from a document, which from memory, and which from interpretation?
chapters.evidence: The four cards distinguish evidence types; they are not a vote on which story is true. Full scans of Anna’s relevant letter and the census have not been verified here. No substitute archive pages have been invented.

chapters.title: Art Before Painting
chapters.subtitle: Learning to Look in the Art Trade
chapters.kicker: OPTIONAL BRANCH · NOT A LATER TURNING POINT
paragraphs: Before choosing art as a vocation, Vincent worked in the business of selling pictures.
His London correspondence discusses paintings, engravings and photographic reproductions. It also reveals a young man forming preferences and sharing them with his brother.

sections.title: Business and Enthusiasm
paragraphs: On 19 November 1873, Vincent wrote to Theo about their work for the same firm. He compared the demand for different reproductions, noted sales of engravings after Ingres, and discussed the success of photographs, especially coloured ones.
He also encouraged Theo to visit museums and read about art. Business and enthusiasm appear together: the letter does not present him as someone who had already rejected the art trade.
In April 1874, he mentioned sending Theo a photographic reproduction of Gustave Jean Jacquet’s Girl Holding a Sword. Published by Goupil & Cie, the photograph survives in Theo’s scrapbook.
Placed beside the letter, it offers a concrete example of a picture passing between the brothers. Consider it not as an early Van Gogh work, but as something he chose to share.

quote.text: You must write me sometime whom you like best among the older painters as well as among the moderns.
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 19 November 1873 · Letter 15

chapters.prompt: Before asking what Vincent painted, ask what he chose to look at—and what he wanted someone else to see.
chapters.evidence: The reproduction is after Jacquet’s 1872 painting, not a Van Gogh painting or a portrait of Eugénie. This branch can be visited from the first two chapters without implying that an interest in art followed a rejection.

chapters.title: Turning to Faith
chapters.subtitle: Reading, Teaching and a Possible Vocation
chapters.imageCaption: Vincent van Gogh, aged nineteen. Photograph by J. M. W. de Louw, The Hague, January 1873. This earlier portrait is not a photograph of his religious work in 1876.
chapters.imageCredit: J. M. W. de Louw · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: After the art trade, Vincent explored teaching and religious work. In England in 1876, he worked in schools and became involved in preaching. His letter to Theo of 3 November describes his first sermon and includes its text.

Religion offered a possible direction, but the route was not straightforward. Further study and training preceded his move to the Belgian mining region. Read these changes as successive efforts to find a vocation, rather than as a single consequence of the London attachment.
chapters.prompt: What kind of work might give a life purpose?
chapters.evidence: An independent curatorial summary, grounded in the linked letters and institutional chronology. The portrait dates from January 1873; it is not evidence of an event in 1876. No single psychological cause is asserted.

chapters.title: Among the Miners
chapters.subtitle: Work, Hardship and an Unsettled Direction
chapters.imageCaption: Miners, Cuesmes. Catalogued as 1880 at the linked image source. A reproduction of a drawing, not a photograph of the miners.
chapters.imageCredit: Vincent van Gogh · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: In December 1878, Vincent wrote to Theo from Wasmes in the Borinage. He described a landscape shaped by coal mining and the difficult conditions in which local people lived and worked.

Religious work did not become a lasting vocation. The mining region also belongs to the years in which he began to give drawing a more deliberate place in his life. The letter and the drawing offer different kinds of evidence: an account addressed to his brother, and a visual study of working people.
chapters.prompt: How does looking closely differ from telling someone else’s story?
chapters.evidence: The accompanying image is a drawing reproduction labelled Miners, Cuesmes at its source, not a photograph or a reconstructed scene. Contemporary letters should be distinguished from later interpretations of these years.

chapters.title: Learning to Draw
chapters.subtitle: Looking Closely, Learning Slowly
chapters.imageCaption: Road in Etten, 1881. Chalk, pencil, pastel and watercolour; underdrawing in pen and brown ink. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1975.1.774.
chapters.imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 459193
paragraphs: Drawing became a practice to be pursued, not simply an interest. In his letter to Theo of 24 September 1880, Vincent discussed exercises and the work of learning. Observation, copying and repeated study formed part of that process.

The early works bring us close to the work of learning. Open a drawing to explore its materials, its setting and the evidence behind its story. Road in Etten belongs to the Early Works section of this first hall; further drawings and paintings continue in Hall 02.
chapters.prompt: What changes when a familiar road becomes something to study?
chapters.evidence: This section uses the September 1880 letter and the museum record for Road in Etten. The work is dated 1881; it is not presented as an illustration made for that particular letter.
